# Race injectors, third person, and the smaller fixes

Everything in one batch that is not karma.

---

## Race injectors

Phoenix's `drugs_simple` has three of these — a behemoth, a centaur and a unity
behemoth — each an aid item whose effect calls `nut.races:transform`: freeze the
player, scale the model, throw an effect every second for nine seconds, then
swap the race.

**Two per race, for all forty-four**, generated by
`_docs/tools/geninjectors.py` from the roster in `schema/races/` — so a new race
is a new pair of items the moment the generator runs.

| | |
|---|---|
| **permanent** | the character *is* that race afterwards, written to the database like any other race change |
| **temporary** | it lasts **one life** - you are a deathclaw until something kills you |

A life is the better unit than a clock, and it is Phoenix's: it makes the thing
an event with an ending you can see coming, rather than a timer nobody can read
running out mid-fight. `injectorDuration` is still there for a server that wants
a deadline, and an item may carry its own `duration`; 0 in both means one life.

**Not everything is an injector.** You do not inject somebody into being a
Securitron, so the nine robot races get a **Conversion Kit** instead, and the
human item is an **Anti-Mutagen Serum** — turning back into a human is a cure
rather than a dose. The temporary versions are *Unstable*, which is both the
mechanic and the flavour.

### They are aid items

`items/base/sh_injector.lua` has `base_aid` as its **own** base — a base item may
itself have a base, which `sh_plant.lua` already does. That inherits Use, the
five-second staring Inject that puts one into somebody else, the per-race chem
whitelists, the power-armour rule, the sound and the screen flash. None of that
is about races, and none of it is written twice.

**Injecting somebody else needs them restrained** (`injectorNeedsRestrained`).
A chem can be pushed into anybody who will stand still for five seconds, which
is fine for a stimpak and not fine for something that rewrites what they are for
good. It says what a consent prompt would say without a prompt: if they did not
agree to this, somebody had to tie them up first. The menu entry is *hidden*
rather than refused, because the answer never changes while you are looking at
them.

### The transformation

Frozen for `injectorTransformTime` (9s, Phoenix's), model scaling toward the new
race's own scale, a beat every second, then the change.

**The effect is drawn, not spawned.** Phoenix use `util.Effect("VortDispel")`
with `ambient/machines/thumper_hit.wav` under it — the "womb, womb" — and
neither is on this server: that sound is Half-Life 2 (gotcha 16) and a missing
effect fails silently. So it is `render.SetColorMaterial` with `DrawSphere` and
`DrawWireframeSphere`, which are engine primitives and need no content at all: a
shell of light that swells and collapses on every beat, a `DynamicLight` on the
ground, and a screen shake that falls off with distance.

The sound is `phoenix/ui/nv/ui_karma_down.mp3` **pitched down to 60 and falling
to 35** across the nine beats. That is the whole trick — a short descending tone
played low is a thump, and one a second that gets deeper plainly builds towards
something.

### Going back

A temporary injection writes `raceRevert = {race, at}` onto the character.
`at` of **0** is the one-life kind: `PlayerDeath` sets a flag and the next
`PlayerSpawn` reverts. The flag matters - `ix.races.Apply` respawns people to
rebuild their hull, so *every* race change fires `PlayerSpawn`, and without it
an injection would undo itself half a second after it landed.

`at` as an `os.time` deadline is the other kind, restored by a one-second tick
over players. `PlayerLoadedCharacter` checks on the way in, because a deadline
usually passes while somebody is offline - and a life-long one ends there too,
since coming back days later as whatever you were injected with is the
temporary version being permanent.

**Not a timer per injection**, for the reason the plants and the cap stashes
both learned: a `CurTime` timer dies with the map, so a race would outlive its
deadline across a restart and become permanent by accident.

**A race change no longer teleports you.** `Spawn` sends a player to a spawn
point, which is right for dying and wrong for this: the position, view angles
and health are taken before and put back on the next frame, because
`PlayerLoadout` and the spawn point selection both run after `Spawn` returns.
Health is clamped to the new race's maximum - races have different base health,
and a radroach with a super mutant's hit points is not what anybody meant.

`ix.races.Apply` is the one implementation of a race change, shared with
`/charsetrace`: the gender fix for male-only creature races, the respawn that
rebuilds hull and view offset, the body-state rebuild, and the explicit save
that `SetRace` does not do.

## Third person

**edunad's Simple Thirdperson**, installed at `addons/simplethirdperson` - the
one that was asked for, Apache 2.0, with its LICENSE beside it. It is a
self-contained `lua/autorun` file with no dependencies, so it is within the
addon rules in `02-server-setup.md`: what those forbid is a Lua addon whose
dependencies are missing.

It has what Helix's built-in one does not: a settings menu on the context
wheel, shoulder view with its own offsets, smoothing per axis, and **server
convars that cap how far anybody may push the camera**
(`simple_thirdperson_maxdistance` and the rest) - which is the part a server
owner cares about.

**Helix's own is turned off and left registered.** Two third person cameras
both writing `CalcView` is one camera fighting itself; theirs only acts when
the `thirdperson` config is on, so `SetDefault` + `ForceSet` to false is the
whole of it. Turning it on in the terminal is how a server drops the addon and
goes back to the built-in one - and that is why the flip is done that way
rather than by re-registering the config, which does nothing: `ix.config.Add`
keeps the first registration's value and Helix's plugins load first.

`/thirdperson` toggles it, `/thirdpersonmenu` opens the settings, and `stp`,
`fo_thirdperson` and `simple_thirdperson_menu` do the same from console.

---

## Container sizes

`ix.container.stored` is a fixed table in the framework, and "how much does a
wooden crate hold" is an economy decision. The dev terminal → WORLD → CONTAINERS
lists every container model with a `WIDTHxHEIGHT` box.

Overrides are kept **apart from the defaults** in `sh_containers.lua`: the
defaults are a statement about Helix's numbers and belong in code, an override
is a decision somebody made at runtime and belongs in the save. Mixed together,
a later change to a default would silently do nothing because the file still
held the old value.

**A change reaches placed containers on the next restart.** Helix restores a
container's inventory with `Restore(id, width, height)` read from the definition,
so the grid follows — but only when it is next restored. Anything already
outside a *smaller* new grid stops being drawn rather than being deleted.

The sizes are synced to clients, because `ix.container.stored` exists on both
realms and the terminal reads its rows from it.

---

## Capture benches start the session unheld

The same rule the capture points follow. A bench is held by whoever last stood
at it long enough to take it, and carrying that across a restart means a faction
that logged off at three in the morning still owns the workshop at noon.

`owner` is still written to the save — it costs nothing and it is the only
record of who had it when the server went down — and thrown away on load.

---

## The look-at tooltip

Helix positions it from the far **edge** of the entity's bounding box, clamped
to the right-hand side of the screen. The closer you stand to something the
further right the label goes, and a workbench you are standing at fills the
view — which pins the label to the edge of the monitor with a tracer line
running the whole way across.

It is now a fixed distance from the entity's **centre**, flipping to the left
when there is no room on the right. Wrapped rather than replaced, so cursor
tooltips and the raised-weapon position are untouched.

---

## Dev terminal buttons

Every width in that file was a guess somebody made by eye, and "CONFIGURE" came
out as "CONFIGU…" — Derma ellipsises with no error and no clue which button it
happened to. The number at the call site is now a **minimum** and the text is
measured against `UI_Bold` (which is what `ixFOButton` sets in its own `Init`);
whichever is larger wins. Row buttons are also centred, which they never were:
`ixFOButton` defaults to left alignment because that is right for the menu's
tall buttons, and every row button inherited it.

---

## Test bot loadouts

The BOTS page used to spawn exactly one armour, which is right for "what does
50% resistance feel like" and useless for "what does *this* loadout stop" — the
thing being tested is usually the sum. There is now a loadout built slot by
slot, with the head and body pools totalled and each clamped the way
`armorMaxResistance` clamps them, and SPAWN dresses a bot in the whole set.

A power armour helmet still pulls its suit in automatically, because a helmet
without one is refused by the armour rules and a bot standing there in its
underwear looks like a bug rather than the rule it is.

## Everything else in that batch

**The mid-air T-pose.** Jumping with anything drawn T-posed until you landed.
It was never physics: the animation tree keys jumping under the string `jump`
and the translator only looked up `tree[act]`, so `ACT_MP_JUMP` found nothing
and fell through to HL2 activities the New Vegas models do not have - sequence
0 on those is the reference pose. See gotcha 21.

**Linked shop stocks.** An entry can name other entries in the same shop that a
purchase also draws from, so "we have thirty rifles" stops meaning thirty of
*each* rifle. Phoenix do it with stock pools referenced by id; links are the
same idea written on the entry that has it, with no pool to garbage collect.
They are deliberately **one-way** - linking the rifle to the pistol does not
link the pistol back, because those are two decisions. Edited with SHARED STOCK
in `/shopconfig`.

**Command exclusions.** The rank override sets a floor, and a floor is a
ladder: everybody above it gets in. An exclusion is the exception a ladder
cannot express - "moderators and above, except the event team" - so it is a
second table, asked **first**, and absolute. You cannot exclude a rank at or
above your own, for the same reason you cannot assign one. EXCLUDE sits beside
SET on the admin menu's COMMANDS page, and excluded ranks are named on the row.

**`/ammo`** gives yourself rounds; with no arguments it lists the types, which
are built from the ammunition items so they cannot drift from what a gun will
actually draw from. **`/forceid`** gives an admin the identity of whoever they
are looking at - one way, and it tells the other person nothing.
**`/benchfactiontoggle`** closes a captured bench to your own faction and opens
it again; it answers to *who took it* rather than to rank, and it is cleared
when the bench changes hands, is released, or the server restarts.

**A stranger still has a description.** Helix's recognition plugin replaces the
description of anybody you do not know with "You do not recognize this person",
which is the wrong way round: the *name* is what you have to be told, and the
description is what you can see with your own eyes. Hiding it leaves a stranger
as a blank label with nothing to roleplay against. The plugin's hook is replaced
through `HOOKS_CACHE` - see gotcha 22 - because a plugin's hook beats the
schema's and cannot be overridden any other way.

**Armour is cut for a kind of body.** `human`, `robot` or `creature`, set with
`ITEM.wearer` or the shorthand `ITEM.isNonHuman`, against a race's kind from
`ix.armor.raceKinds`. A suit made for a person will not go onto a deathclaw or
a securitron. Naming a race in `armorRace` overrides it - an armour that names
deathclaws was made for deathclaws - and `armorRaceKinds` turns the whole rule
off for a server that finds it strands somebody.

**The bot armour picker scrolls.** It was a `DermaMenu` capped at sixty entries
because Derma menus have no scrollbar and run off the screen, which meant most
of the roster could not be chosen. It is a window with a search box now, and
the cap is gone.
